Martha Ballard was a midwife who lived in Maine. At the age of 50, she began a diary, which she maintained for 27 years until her death. In this diary, Ballard kept a brief record of her daily activities, including visits to women in childbirth and ailing neighbors, and also the comings and goings of family members, friends, and neighbors. The historian Laurel Thatcher Ulrich used the diary to write a biography of Ballard entitled A Midwife’s Tale (1990) that was awarded the Pulitzer Prize and several other awards. On July 12, 1893, a young scholar named Frederick Jackson Turner gave an address to a meeting of the American Historical Association at the World Columbian Exposition in Chicago. His talk was entitled “The Significance of the Frontier in American History.” Here Turner laid the foundation for his famous “Frontier Thesis,” which argued that the frontier experience was the most important force shaping American life. He wrote, “The frontier is the line of most rapid and effective Americanization. American social development has been continually beginning over again on the frontier. This perennial rebirth, this fluidity of American life, this expansion westward with its new opportunities, its continuous touch with the simplicity of primitive society, furnish the forces dominating American character . …” Turner’s thesis made him one of the most influential historians in American history. Why did Turner’s view of Western history prove so compelling to his contemporaries?
